terms.gloss: bring in, introduce (a custom, an idea)
terms.grammar: verb, third conjugation, transitive; with in and the accusative
evidence: Cic. Tusc. 5.10: in domūs etiam intrōdūxit
terms.comment: Lewis & Short: “to bring in, introduce … to institute, originate”: cōnsuētūdinem intrōdūcere.

evidence: Cic. Rab. Post. 9 (Lewis & Short): mōrem novōrum jūdiciōrum in rem pūblicam
Aug. Conf. 9.7.15: ut canerentur … īnstitūtum est

phrases.latin: Sōcratēs autem prīmus philosophiam dēvocāvit ē caelō et in urbibus conlocāvit et in domūs etiam intrōdūxit
phrases.english: Socrates was the first to call philosophy down from the sky; he settled it in cities and even brought it into people’s homes.

phrases.latin: hāc intrōductā cōnsuētūdine saepe īnscientibus nōbīs et cēnantibus obrēpit
phrases.english: Now that this has become our custom, he often steals in on us unannounced while we are at dinner.

phrases.latin: tunc hymnī et psalmī ut canerentur secundum mōrem orientālium partium, nē populus maerōris taediō contābēsceret, īnstitūtum est
phrases.english: It was then that the singing of hymns and psalms after the custom of the East was introduced, so that the people should not waste away in weariness and grief.

sources: Lewis & Short: introduco · Lewis & Short: induco · Lewis & Short: instituo
John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, p. 334.
Quotations from the Latinitas loci collections (loci-augustinus), checked against the editions named there.

Quotations marked “Lewis & Short” are given as Lewis & Short cites them, with its references, in the house spelling (macrons, consonantal j); they have not been checked against a modern edition.
